title: Pythagoras’ Theorem

findings.finding: Ask students to explain why the non-right investigation triangle does not contradict Pythagoras’ theorem.
findings.breakdown: This connects the numerical investigation to the theorem’s right-angle condition.
findings.checked: Triangle 4 gives 5.4² + 7.5² = 85.41, whereas 8² = 64. The statement in p6-theorem-introduction applies only to right-angled triangles. The task requires only that statement and the completed investigation.
findings.assumptions: Students have completed the investigation and read the theorem.

repair.proposal: After p7-q2, offer: “A student says, ‘Triangle 4 has 5.4² + 7.5² ≠ 8², so Pythagoras’ theorem is wrong.’ Explain the mistake using the theorem’s opening sentence and the investigation table.” Expected answer: the theorem concerns right-angled triangles; triangle 4 is not right-angled, so its unequal totals do not contradict it.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the scope of the theorem rather than merely repeat the unequal calculations.

findings.finding: Unknown-side calculations and the choice between two possible hypotenuses are required before either application has been taught.
findings.breakdown: Students must construct two equations, use addition or subtraction to isolate the unknown square, take its positive root, and apply the whole-number condition. Assigning the unknown automatically to the hypotenuse misses valid shorter-side solutions.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching checks complete triples or scales known triples. p6-write-d-node and p6-write-f-node ask only for equations. p13-q4 supplies generating formulas, not an unknown-side method. The explicit unknown-side teaching in p16 and p20 comes after these tasks. Asking for two answers in p14-q5 signals the issue but does not teach how to obtain them.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary algebra and square roots may be prior knowledge. A calculator is assumed for decimal roots; it does not supply the hypotenuse assignments.

repair.proposal: Before p14-q5, add: “(6,10,x) satisfies Pythagoras’ theorem. Find the possible positive lengths x. If x is longest, x² = 6² + 10² = 136, so x = √136 ≈ 11.66. If 10 is longest, 6² + x² = 10², so x² = 64 and x = 8. The side 6 cannot be longest because 10 is larger. Both lengths satisfy the theorem, but only 8 gives a whole-number triad.”

findings.doneWhen: Both hypotenuse assignments, the corresponding calculations and the whole-number filter are demonstrated before p14-q5.

findings.finding: Investigate which whole-number divisors preserve whole-number entries when reducing a triad.
findings.breakdown: This develops the whole-number restriction in the taught scaling rule.
findings.checked: The common positive whole-number divisors of 90, 400 and 410 are exactly 1, 2, 5 and 10. Dividing by 10 gives (9,40,41), which has no common integer divisor greater than 1. The task uses the division and whole-number checks already required in p11.
findings.assumptions: Students can identify factors of whole numbers; no formal greatest-common-divisor algorithm is required.

repair.proposal: After p11-generating-guided-b, offer: “For (90,400,410), list every positive whole number by which you can divide all three entries and still obtain whole numbers. Which resulting triad has the smallest entries? Explain why it cannot be reduced further by a whole-number divisor greater than 1.” Expected answer: divisors 1, 2, 5 and 10; smallest resulting triad (9,40,41), with no common divisor greater than 1.

findings.doneWhen: Students connect allowable division to the requirement that every entry remain a whole number.

findings.finding: Keep the hypotenuse fixed while increasing one known leg.
findings.breakdown: The comparison exposes how increasing one leg decreases the other and makes the exchange of leg roles visible.
findings.checked: For hypotenuse 13, known legs 5, 9 and 12 give other legs 12, √88 and 5 respectively. All are positive and shorter than the hypotenuse. The follow-up gives √(17²−8²) = 15. p20 teaches the required method; p21-q3 has no comparable fixed-hypotenuse run.
findings.assumptions: Exact answers may remain unsimplified roots, consistent with the booklet.

repair.proposal: After p21-q3-block, ask: “Before calculating, predict how the unknown leg changes as the known leg increases. Each right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 13 cm. Find the other leg when the known leg is (a) 5 cm, (b) 9 cm, (c) 12 cm. Give exact answers. What do you notice about (a) and (c)?” Expected answers: 12 cm, √88 cm, 5 cm; the legs exchange roles. The hypotenuse stays fixed and only the known leg varies. Follow with: “A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 17 cm and one leg 8 cm. Find the other leg.” Expected answer: 15 cm.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict and explain the relationship, then apply the method to the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: The isosceles altitude’s base-bisection property is neither rehearsed before the example nor explicitly connected to the substituted half-base.
findings.breakdown: The worked example uses 13.5 cm from a labelled 27 cm base. Without recalling and naming the isosceles property, students cannot justify that leg length and may infer that every perpendicular altitude halves a base.
findings.checked: Matching equal-side ticks are already used in p25-q2-l, so that part of c13 is removed. Neither the preceding strategy teaching nor its supplied exercise rehearses why an isosceles altitude bisects the base. p18-q4-f supplies equal-half marks directly. The p26 demonstration labels the half-base but supplies no connecting sentence; the later guided question’s equal-half marks do not explain the example’s decision.
findings.assumptions: The isosceles altitude property is prior geometry knowledge from the course’s geometry material. The teacher checks review responses. Calculator use does not affect the geometric decision.

repair.proposal: Before p26-information, add: “An isosceles triangle has base 18 cm. A perpendicular is drawn from the vertex between its equal sides to the base. Find the two base segments.” Expected answer: 9 cm each. Repeat with base 7 m; expected answer: 3.5 m each. Ask students to name the property used. In p26-example-content, add before substitution: “The two sloping sides are equal, so the perpendicular altitude bisects the base. Half-base = 27 ÷ 2 = 13.5 cm.”

findings.doneWhen: The review checks recall of base bisection, and the worked example explicitly links that property to 13.5 cm.

findings.finding: Generalise the central length in the right-triangle spiral.
findings.breakdown: Students explain the repeated increase in squared length rather than repeatedly calculate roots.
findings.checked: Starting with squared central length 1, each new perpendicular side of length 1 adds 1 by Pythagoras’ theorem. After n triangles the length is √(n+1); length 5 requires n+1 = 25, hence n = 24. This uses the multistep structure already taught and practised.
findings.assumptions: n is a non-negative integer counting attached triangles; every new unit side is perpendicular to the preceding central segment.

repair.proposal: After p37-q11, offer: “Start with a central segment of length 1 and attach n successive right triangles, each with a new outer side of length 1 perpendicular to the preceding central segment. Predict the final central length before calculating. Explain your rule, then determine how many triangles produce a central length of 5.” Expected answer: √(n+1), because each triangle adds 1 to the preceding squared length; 24 triangles produce length 5.

findings.doneWhen: Students justify the rule through successive squared lengths and correctly interpret the triangle count.

contextQuestions.question: Have students already been taught arc length as θ/360 × 2πr and how to find a composite shape’s perimeter while excluding shared internal edges? The supplied Pythagoras teaching does not teach these methods; the course-library titles do not establish whether students have studied them. If they have not, these tasks need a teaching bridge before p34-q4-d.

protectedGroups.observation: The hypotenuse is identified by its position opposite the right angle, regardless of the triangle's orientation.
protectedGroups.varies: Orientation, proportions and the position of the marked right angle, including horizontal hypotenuses.
protectedGroups.invariant: Each figure is a triangle with a marked right angle and exactly one opposite side.

protectedGroups.observation: The side opposite the right angle remains the hypotenuse when the triangle's orientation changes.
protectedGroups.invariant: Three labelled sides, an explicit right-angle marker and the task of writing the squared relationship.

protectedGroups.observation: The same theorem applies to an explicitly marked right triangle embedded in a larger figure.
protectedGroups.varies: The surrounding figure: rectangle, semicircle and cylinder.
protectedGroups.invariant: A supplied right triangle with labelled legs and hypotenuse; only its equation is required.

protectedGroups.observation: Common scaling preserves the right-angle relationship, including when the lengths cease to be whole numbers.
protectedGroups.invariant: Corresponding side ratios remain 3:4:5 and the triangles remain right-angled.

protectedGroups.observation: Exact hypotenuse answers may be whole numbers or roots; doubling both legs doubles the hypotenuse.
protectedGroups.varies: One leg changes at each adjacent step; from the first to the third task both legs double.
protectedGroups.invariant: Right-angle position, unknown hypotenuse and addition shortcut.

protectedGroups.observation: The role of a given length determines whether its square is added or subtracted.
protectedGroups.varies: 16 changes from a leg to the hypotenuse, and the unknown changes from hypotenuse to leg.
protectedGroups.invariant: Given lengths 16 cm and 12 cm and the right-angle position.

protectedGroups.invariant: Hypotenuse 16 cm, known leg 12 cm and unknown shorter side.

protectedGroups.observation: With the hypotenuse fixed, reducing one leg increases the other.
protectedGroups.varies: Known leg decreases from 12 cm to 8 cm.
protectedGroups.invariant: Hypotenuse 16 cm, unknown left leg and triangle orientation.

protectedGroups.observation: Identical numerical givens require different operations when their side roles change.
protectedGroups.varies: 10 cm changes from hypotenuse to leg; the unknown becomes the hypotenuse.
protectedGroups.invariant: Given lengths 10 cm and 5 cm and upper right-angle position.

protectedGroups.observation: Rotating a triangle leaves the hypotenuse calculation unchanged.
protectedGroups.varies: Orientation and placement of the labelled legs.
protectedGroups.invariant: Perpendicular legs 10 cm and 5 cm and unknown hypotenuse.

protectedGroups.observation: The outer hypotenuse depends on the sum of the three given squared lengths, including when those lengths exchange positions.
protectedGroups.varies: One given length at a time, followed by reassignment of the same lengths to different sides.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two adjoining right triangles, their shared diagonal and the outer hypotenuse as the unknown.

protectedGroups.invariant: A large right triangle containing a smaller right triangle, with the same two numerical givens.
